title: Fresh eyes
bridge: Fresh eyes is like asking a colleague who did not write the code to review it. Except: each reviewer is a separate query() session that gets only its slice. That is the ticket and the diff, or the app and the QA plan. None of them ever sees Nova's transcript.
intro: Models grade their own work too kindly. This lesson adds three readers who never saw Nova's reasoning. A reviewer with Byte's lenses, a scope judge that can veto, and a QA agent that tests the app in a browser. A loop ties them together and keeps a receipt.

sections.h: The scope judge, part 1: what it sees and what it says
p: Start from a real habit. An agent fixes a bug. Then it tidies the function next to it, renames a variable, and loosens a flaky assertion to get green. Each change looks reasonable in the moment. Together they make the PR hard to review.

The scope judge is a reader with no context but the ticket and the diff. It cannot be persuaded by Nova's notes because it never gets them. Its job is one question: does every change serve the ticket? Spotify's judge vetoes about 25% of sessions; that is a reference, not a target.
A rubric judge is a model given a fixed set of rules and asked for a verdict in a fixed shape. The rules are the prompt below; the shape is the ScopeVerdict schema.
sections.because: A judge without Nova's reasoning keeps PRs to the ticket, and its fixed shape lets the loop act on the verdict.

notes.text: A mechanical list of test changes, computed by code: removed assertions, .skip, .only, longer timeouts. The judge gets it as input.
The prompt sets the role: a careful reviewer from another team, with the ticket and the diff only.
The first veto reason: refactors, renames and "while I was here" fixes the ticket did not ask for.
The second: a weaker test. This one is never explained away; Nova restores the test.
Small supporting changes are fine. The judge should not veto a new test ID or a helper the fix needs.
Unsure means pass with a note. Every item cites file and lines, so Nova can act on it.
The verdict: pass or veto, two lists of cited items, and a free note.
The type the self-review loop uses to branch on verdict.

sections.h: The scope judge, part 2: one session, no tools
p: scopeJudge builds one prompt from the ticket, the diff and the test-change list, and runs it as its own query() session. Sonnet 5.5 at medium is the routing table's choice for a rubric judge. No tools: it reads what it was given and answers.

On a veto, Nova gets the reasons. It reverts the unrelated change, or explains why the ticket needs it; the explanation goes into the PR. A second veto on the same item goes to a person instead of another round.
sections.because: We spend one Sonnet call per PR to catch drift that a tired human reviewer would wave through.

notes.text: Three inputs, clearly labelled. The diff is git diff origin/main...HEAD, produced by the harness.
tools: [] and settingSources: []: no repo access, no skills, no memory. The judge cannot wander.
Structured output in the ScopeVerdict shape, so the loop never parses prose.
parse checks the JSON and returns the typed verdict.
No result is an error. The harness retries or flags it; it never assumes a pass.

sections.h: The reviewer, part 1: findings and lenses
p: The reviewer is different from the judge. It does get the approved plan, because it checks the diff against the plan. Is every plan item done? Is there anything the plan did not ask for? It still never sees Nova's transcript or notes.

A lens is a review checklist for one concern. Byte already has them: convention, logic, security and performance for the frontend, and a BE playbook. We bake the same files into the image, so Nova and Byte look for the same things.
Important means correctness, security, a missed requirement, a plan item not done, or a change the plan did not ask for. Everything else is a nit, counted but not fixed one by one.
sections.because: A reviewer that never saw Nova's reasoning finds more, and sharing Byte's lenses means two reviews use one standard.

notes.text: execFile with an argv, never a shell string. The harness runs git; the reviewer does not get git.
Byte's playbook files, copied into the sandbox image at build time (lesson g3-5).
One finding: where, which rule, how severe, and the text. The schema is also what the panel returns (lesson g4-5).
Two severities only. important is fixed or explained; nit is counted.
The structured output wraps findings in an object, which JSON Schema prefers over a bare array.
The prompt names the diff file and the lenses, and says what matters.
No findings is a fine answer. The reviewer is not rewarded for finding something.

sections.h: The reviewer, part 2: read-only, and why no Bash
p: The harness writes the diff to /run/nova/review/diff.patch and starts the reviewer with Read, Grep and Glob only. It can look at any file in the checkout and the lens folder, and it can change nothing.

Bash is refused for a precise reason. git diff --no-index can read any two paths on the machine, and --output= can write a file. Byte's engines.ts warns about the same thing. A read-only reviewer with Bash is not read-only.

Opus 5.5 at medium does the logic and security pass. On a big diff, a second pass on Sonnet 5.5 at low checks conventions. The harness adds a fingerprint per finding and appends them to .nova/review.jsonl.
sections.because: The reviewer must be unable to change anything, so the tool list is short and Bash is out.

notes.text: The harness computes the diff against origin/main. maxBuffer 64 MiB allows a large patch.
The patch is written where the reviewer may read. The reviewer never runs git itself.
Opus 5.5 at medium, the routing table's choice for logic and security.
settingSources ["project"]: frontend/AGENTS.md and the repo's own rules still apply to the review.
Three read tools. Grep and Glob let it look around the diff for context.
Bash is denied by name, along with every write tool and the web.
dontAsk: anything not in allowedTools is refused, not asked about. Nobody is there to answer.
additionalDirectories opens the lens folder and the patch folder for Read.
The caller fingerprints each finding (sha1 of path, rule and normalised message) for the receipt.

p: One review pass leaves things behind. An endless loop wastes money and hides a real disagreement. The loop in between needs memory: which findings were fixed, which were left, and why. That memory is the Receipt.

A fingerprint is a short hash of a finding's path, rule and normalised message. Two findings with the same fingerprint are the same finding, even if the line number moved. The receipt keeps two sets of fingerprints: fixed and left.

The receipt is written to .nova/receipt.json. The PR body shows it as one line: "Found 6 · fixed 5 · left 1, because …". Byte reads it too (lesson g2-5), so it does not repeat findings Nova already handled.
sections.because: Fingerprints let the loop tell real progress from ping-pong, and the receipt tells the human reviewer what was already looked at.

notes.text: fingerprinted adds the sha1 to each finding. reviewPanel is the workflow version for big diffs (lesson g4-5).
NovaSession is G3's harness session: it can ask the model to fix, re-run checks, and ask a human.
found counts every important finding seen, across all rounds.
fixed is derived: the size of the fixed set. A finding is fixed at most once.
left holds pairs of location and reason, for the PR's "left 1, because …" line.
leave records the finding and its fingerprint, so the next round skips it.

sections.h: The loop, part 2: review, fix, re-check, until nothing important is open
p: Each round starts with a review: the single reviewer, or the panel workflow when the plan asked for one. Important findings not already left are handled one by one. Then the checks from checks.json run again, so a fix cannot quietly break a QA check.

A finding whose fingerprint was fixed before and is back is ping-pong. Nova stops fixing it, leaves it with a reason, and asks in the ticket's Slack thread. There is no round cap: the loop ends when nothing important is open or every open item is with a person. G3's progress watcher still steps in if nothing moves.
The scope judge runs once the reviewer is clean. A veto is handled by reverting or explaining; a second veto on the same item goes to a person.
sections.because: No cap, but no loop either: fingerprints end the ping-pong, and people decide the disagreements.

notes.text: while (true) with no counter. The exits are below: nothing important, or every item with a person.
plan.workflow is the plan's own line saying why a panel helps; otherwise one reviewer.
Keep important findings that were not already left. Nits are counted elsewhere.
The normal exit: a clean review.
Seen and fixed before, and back again: ping-pong. The person decides, not another round.
fixOrExplain lets Nova disagree with a reason. The reason lands in the PR.
Re-run the chosen checks after every round of fixes.
Scope judge last, on the final diff, with the ticket only.
handleVeto reverts or explains. A second veto on the same item goes to a person.

sections.h: The QA agent, part 1: a tester who sees only the app
p: Tests can pass while the screen is still wrong. A toast shows while the form still saves. An empty state overlaps the table at 760 pixels. A count is off by one. A tester who looks at the screen catches these.

The QA agent gets the QA plan and the app's URL. It does not get the code, the diff or Nova's notes. For each check it opens a fresh browser context, does what a user would do, and records a short video. Pass only when it saw the expected result itself.
Calibration is a set of 8 to 10 labelled examples that show what a fail looks like. Before the pilot the QA agent must fail every planted-bug case, and its leniency is tracked weekly.
sections.because: The videos are the proof reviewers trust most, and a tester that never saw the code cannot be lenient on purpose.

sections.h: The QA agent, part 2: a browser and one folder
p: qaOptions builds the session options. The model is Sonnet 5.5 at medium, or Opus 5.5 at low when judging screens is the main job. The working directory is /work/.nova/qa, which holds the QA plan and the calibration examples, not the checkout.

Its only tools are Read and the Playwright MCP server, pinned in the image. Bash, Grep, Glob and every write tool are denied, and so is Read on /work/fcp. The app is FCP Lab on the same VM, seeded with fake data. Layout checks run at 760x900 and 1440x900, the two widths from e2e/helpers/responsive.ts.
One decision is still open: the Playwright MCP server or the Playwright CLI for agents, which uses fewer tokens. Check the docs of the pinned version for the exact video flag.
sections.because: A tester with a browser and nothing else is the closest thing to a user, and it cannot peek at the code.

quiz.q: What does the scope judge see?

options.text: The ticket, the diff and a mechanical list of test changes
options.why: Nothing else. Without Nova's notes it cannot be persuaded that a refactor was needed.

options.text: The ticket, the plan and the transcript, for context
options.why: The transcript is exactly what would let Nova's reasoning leak into the verdict.

options.text: Only the diff, so it stays neutral
options.why: Without the ticket it cannot tell which changes serve it.

quiz.q: A finding was fixed in round 1 and comes back in round 2. What does the loop do?

options.text: Fixes it again; the loop has no round cap
options.why: No round cap is true, but a returning fingerprint is ping-pong, not progress.

options.text: Leaves it with a reason and asks a person in the ticket's Slack thread
options.why: fixedPrints remembers the first fix; the second sighting goes to a person.

options.text: Stops the whole run as failed
options.why: One disagreement is not a failed run. The item is listed in the PR as left, with a reason.

quiz.q: Which tools does the QA agent have?

options.text: Read on the checkout and Bash, so it can run the tests
options.why: It runs no tests and never reads the code. Tests passing is not what it checks.

options.text: A browser (the Playwright MCP server) and Read on /work/.nova/qa only
options.why: It sees the app and the QA plan, like a user with a checklist.

options.text: The same tools as Nova, with a different prompt
options.why: A different prompt is not fresh eyes. The tool list is what keeps it blind to the code.
